1793-1854

Caption This

The Early Republic and the Market Economy

5

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

Monticello, Jefferson’s home

Not done

What you’re looking at: A painting from Norton Ch. 7. A big red-brick house with a white-columned porch and a round dome stands at the back of a wide green lawn with tall trees. Two women in light dresses walk on the lawn. A boy rolls a hoop. A man in a tall hat sits at the lower left.

Heads up: Monticello was Thomas Jefferson’s home, and enslaved people worked there. Aim your joke at the big house, the dome, or a leader with big plans. Never joke about enslaved people.

  • Look at the size of the house and the lawn. What does it say about the person who lived here?
  • Jefferson wanted a small national government, but he made a very big land deal. How do those two ideas fit together?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Louisiana Purchase (1803)Marbury v. Madison (1803)Lewis and Clark expedition (1804-1806)
Image 2 of 5

The turtle cartoon about the embargo

Not done

What you’re looking at: A hand-colored cartoon from Norton Ch. 7. A big turtle bites the back of a man’s pants as he runs. The man hugs a barrel marked SUPERFINE and shouts, “Oh! this cursed Ograbme.” (Ograbme is embargo spelled backward.) Another man sits on the turtle’s back and laughs. A paper marked LICENCE lies on the grass. On the right, men load barrels near a ship with British flags.

Heads up: This cartoon makes fun of a law. Aim your joke at the turtle, the barrel, or the law. Do not joke about sailors or merchants as a group.

  • Read the speech bubbles. Why does the man call it “cursed Ograbme”? (Hint: read it backward.)
  • Look at the ships and the barrel. What do you think the man is trying to do?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Embargo Act (1807)War of 1812 (1812-1815)
Image 3 of 5

The handwritten Star-Spangled Banner

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photo of a handwritten page, from Norton Ch. 7. The page has four verses in old, slanted handwriting. You can read “O say can you see,” “the star-spangled banner,” and “the land of the free & the home of the brave.” A few words are crossed out. A stamp in the lower left corner says COPYRIGHT 1908.

Heads up: These are the real words of the national anthem. Aim your joke at the old handwriting, the crossed-out words, or how hard it is to write a song. Never joke about soldiers or about people who were hurt in the war.

  • Read the first two lines. What do you think the writer saw by “the dawn’s early light”?
  • Look at the crossed-out words. What does a messy draft tell you about how the song was written?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: War of 1812 (1812-1815)Treaty of Ghent (1814)Battle of New Orleans (1814-1815)
Image 4 of 5

Steamboats at a river landing

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photo from Norton Ch. 8. Two big steamboats with tall smokestacks are tied up at a muddy riverbank, and dark smoke rises from them. On the shore are mule and horse wagons, stacks of hay bales, barrels, and many people. This photo was taken after the years of this lesson (the mark in the corner says Detroit Publishing Co.), but it shows the kind of river landing Norton describes.

Heads up: People are working on the shore. Aim your joke at the boats, the smoke, the mud, or the crowded dock. Never joke about the workers.

  • Look at the smoke and the wagons. What do you think the boats and wagons carried? How could they work together?
  • Norton says steamboats could travel both ways on a river. Why would that matter to farmers and traders?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: steamboatsmarket economyErie Canal (1825)
Image 5 of 5

Two women mill workers with shuttles

Not done

What you’re looking at: A hand-colored photo from Norton Ch. 8. Two women stand side by side in long dresses and white aprons. One wears a patterned dress, and the other wears a dark top and skirt. Each one holds a long wooden shuttle, a tool used to weave cloth on a loom. Norton’s picture description calls them mill workers.

Heads up: These are real working women. Write one clear line about their work or about what the photo shows. No jokes about the women, their clothes, or their looks.

  • Look at what each woman holds. What kind of work did they do?
  • Norton says women were the first factory workers in the nation. Where did many of them come from?
